script.title: Schedule C explained, section by section, for freelancers
script.hook: If you freelance as a sole proprietor, Schedule C is the heart of your tax return. It decides your profit, and your profit decides most of your tax. Yet most people only ever see it through tax software, clicking next. In this video we'll walk through the whole form, section by section, with one example freelancer, so you know what every part means and where your numbers come from. Twenty twenty-six returns, filed in twenty twenty-seven. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you freelance as a sole proprietor, Schedule C is the heart of your tax return. It decides your profit, and your profit decides most of your tax. Yet most people only ever see it through tax software, clicking next. In this video we'll walk through the whole form, section by section, with one example freelancer, so you know what every part means and where your numbers come from. Twenty twenty-six returns, filed in twenty twenty-seven. Education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding a large form with a coral C on a navy background. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Meet Jo
segments.narration: Meet Jo, a fictional freelance copywriter. In twenty twenty-six, clients paid Jo sixty-eight thousand dollars. Jo refunded one client five hundred dollars. Jo's business expenses came to about seven and a half thousand, and Jo works from a qualifying home office. We'll fill in Jo's Schedule C as we go, and by the end you'll see how the form gets from sixty-eight thousand of payments to the profit that's actually taxed.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a simple profile card with a pen and coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Header
segments.narration: The top of the form is about the business itself. Your name, the business name if you use one, and a six-digit principal business code that describes what you do, from a list in the instructions. An EIN if you have one; a sole proprietor can leave it blank. Your business address if it's different from home. And your accounting method. Like most freelancers, Jo ticks cash: income counts when it's received and expenses when they're paid.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form header with small boxes highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Questions
segments.narration: Then a few yes or no questions. Did you materially participate in the business? For a freelancer who does the work, that's almost always yes. Did you start or buy the business this year? And did you make any payments that would require you to file ten ninety-nines, and if so, did you file them? Answer honestly. If you paid a contractor two thousand dollars or more directly and didn't send the form, the fix is to send it, not to tick no.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two tick boxes with a pencil. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Income
segments.narration: Part one is income. Line one is gross receipts: everything clients paid you during the year, gross of platform fees. Jo's is sixty-eight thousand, from Jo's income log, cross-checked against the ten ninety-nines Jo received. Then returns and allowances, which is refunds you gave: five hundred. Cost of goods sold only applies if you sell products, so Jo leaves it at zero. That gives gross income of sixty-seven thousand five hundred.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a small coin going back. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Expenses overview
segments.narration: Part two is expenses, and it's where most of the work is. The form lists categories: advertising, car and truck, commissions and fees, contract labor, depreciation, insurance, legal and professional, office expense, rent, repairs, supplies, taxes and licenses, travel, meals, utilities, and other expenses. You don't need to fit every cost perfectly; you need each one in a sensible category, consistently, with a record behind it. If something could fit two categories, like a software subscription that's also an office expense, pick one and use it every year. Consistency matters more than the perfect box, and it makes year-to-year comparisons meaningful.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a row of colored folders. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jo's expenses
segments.narration: Here's Jo's year. Commissions and fees, mostly payment processor fees: one thousand nine hundred. Car and truck: twelve hundred miles to client meetings at seventy-two and a half cents, eight hundred seventy. Legal and professional, Jo's accountant: four hundred. Utilities, the business share of phone and internet: nine hundred sixty. Supplies and a new monitor under the small-item threshold: six hundred. And other expenses, listed by name: software subscriptions two thousand one hundred, a writing course four hundred, bank fees one hundred twenty. Total: about seven thousand three hundred fifty.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. receipts sorting into folders. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Meals and travel
segments.narration: Two categories have special rules worth knowing. Business meals, like lunch with a client where you discuss work, are generally only fifty percent deductible, and you need a note of who and why. Travel means trips away from home overnight for business: flights, lodging, local transport. Jo didn't travel this year, but if you did, keep the itinerary with the receipts, because mixed business and vacation trips have their own rules.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a half-filled plate and a suitcase. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Depreciation
segments.narration: Bigger equipment, like a computer or a camera, usually goes on the depreciation line through Form forty-five sixty-two. Under current rules most equipment can be deducted in full in the year you start using it, either with section one seventy-nine or bonus depreciation, rather than spread over years. Small items can usually be expensed directly as supplies if you use the de minimis safe harbor. Software will ask you which; if you're unsure, that's a good question for a preparer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop with a small calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Home office
segments.narration: After the expense categories, there's a separate line for the home office. Jo uses the simplified method: a hundred twenty square feet times five dollars, six hundred dollars. With the regular method, Jo would fill in Form eighty-eight twenty-nine instead and carry the result here. The home office line comes after tentative profit because the deduction can't be more than the business's income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a desk inside a small house outline. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Net profit
segments.narration: So Jo's net profit is gross income of sixty-seven thousand five hundred, minus seven thousand three hundred fifty of expenses, minus six hundred for the home office: about fifty-nine thousand five hundred fifty. That number goes two places. To Schedule one, as business income on the ten forty. And to Schedule SE, where self-employment tax is calculated. Everything else on Jo's return builds from it. If you have more than one client, it can be useful to see profit by client too, which your income log can show, but the form only needs the total.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with two arrows leading away. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What follows
segments.narration: From there, Schedule SE turns Jo's profit into about eight thousand four hundred self-employment tax. Half of that comes off income on Schedule one. The qualified business income deduction on Form eighty-nine ninety-five takes off up to twenty percent more. Then the standard deduction and the brackets produce Jo's income tax. Jo's four estimated payments are entered as payments already made, and the return shows what's left to pay or refund.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small flowchart of forms. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Let's talk about what sits behind each line, because Schedule C itself doesn't include receipts. You keep them. For income, that's your income log, your invoices, and the ten ninety-nines. For each expense category, it's the receipt or bank line plus a short note on the business purpose, especially for anything that could look personal. For the car, the mileage log. For the home office, a floor plan and a photo. The general rule is to keep records for at least three years after you file, longer for equipment you're still depreciating. If you keep these as you go, Schedule C is simply adding up totals.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a neat folder with tabs for each category. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two businesses
segments.narration: What if you have two different businesses, say copywriting and selling prints online? Generally each separate business gets its own Schedule C, with its own income, expenses and business code. Two kinds of similar work under one business, like writing and editing, usually stay on one. And if you're married and both freelance, each spouse files their own Schedule C and Schedule SE, because self-employment tax is figured per person, for Social Security credit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two small forms side by side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: The Schedule C mistakes we see most: reporting net deposits instead of gross receipts, which can look like missing income next to a ten ninety-nine K. Putting personal costs in business categories. Forgetting expenses paid from a personal card. Claiming a home office that isn't used exclusively for work. And guessing round numbers without records. Each one is avoidable with an income log, an expense log and a monthly ten-minute check.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. five small crossed-out icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: the header describes your business, part one is your income from your own log, part two sorts expenses into categories, the home office has its own line, and the bottom line, net profit, drives both your self-employment tax and your income tax. Keep the logs all year and this form takes an hour. The Quarterly Tax Tracker in the description has income, expense and mileage logs that line up with these categories. script.title: The home office deduction: every rule, both methods, real numbers
script.hook: The home office deduction has a reputation: either it's a red flag that gets you audited, or it's a huge write-off everyone should take. Neither is quite right. In this video we'll go through who qualifies, the tests, both ways to calculate it with real numbers for a renter and a homeowner, what you can and can't include, the catch for homeowners, and the records that make it solid. Twenty twenty-six rules. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: The home office deduction has a reputation: either it's a red flag that gets you audited, or it's a huge write-off everyone should take. Neither is quite right. In this video we'll go through who qualifies, the tests, both ways to calculate it with real numbers for a renter and a homeowner, what you can and can't include, the catch for homeowners, and the records that make it solid. Twenty twenty-six rules. Education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes at a desk inside a small house on a navy background. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Who
segments.narration: First, who can take it. Self-employed people, including freelancers and side hustlers filing Schedule C. Employees working from home for an employer currently can't deduct a home office on their federal return, even if they have a dedicated room. So if you have a job and a side business, the deduction relates to the business only, and the space has to qualify for the business. And if you have a W-2 job but also a real freelance business you run from the same desk, the business use has to meet the tests on its own; your employer's work there doesn't count toward it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two figures, one with a briefcase greyed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Exclusive
segments.narration: Test one: exclusive use. The space must be used only for your business. It doesn't need to be a whole room; a clearly defined area, like a corner with your desk, can count, but nothing else can happen there. The guest bed in the office, the kids doing homework at your desk, the family computer: those break exclusivity. There are narrow exceptions, like storing inventory or running a daycare, but for most freelancers, only means only.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a desk with a small fence around it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Regular and principal
segments.narration: Test two: regular use, meaning ongoing, not occasional. Test three: it's your principal place of business. That's met if you do most of your work there, or if it's where you do your admin and management and there's no other fixed place where you do those tasks. A freelancer who meets clients at cafes but does all the invoicing, planning and writing at home usually passes. Alternatively, it qualifies if you regularly meet clients there, or it's a separate structure like a detached studio.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a house with a star and a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Simplified
segments.narration: Now the two methods. The simplified method: five dollars per square foot of office, up to three hundred square feet, so a maximum of fifteen hundred dollars. No depreciation, no bills to total, no extra form. You just need the measurement and to meet the tests. A hundred twenty square foot office gives six hundred dollars. At sixty thousand of profit, a deduction of that size saves roughly a hundred forty dollars of federal tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tape measure and a small tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Regular renter
segments.narration: The regular method uses your actual costs. Take the office's share of your home: a hundred twenty square feet of a nine hundred sixty square foot apartment is twelve and a half percent. Then add up the home's yearly costs: rent of twenty-one thousand six hundred, utilities of two thousand eight hundred eighty, renter's insurance of two hundred forty, about twenty-four thousand seven hundred twenty. Twelve and a half percent of that is about three thousand ninety dollars. Five times the simplified method, worth around seven hundred dollars of tax at sixty thousand of profit.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a floor plan with one room shaded and a pile of bills. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Regular owner
segments.narration: For a homeowner, rent is replaced by mortgage interest, property tax, home insurance, utilities and repairs, plus depreciation on the office's share of the building, not the land. Say the office is ten percent of the home, and interest, tax, insurance and utilities total twenty thousand: that's two thousand, plus a depreciation amount on ten percent of the building's value spread over thirty-nine years. The mortgage interest and property tax you don't use here can still go on Schedule A if you itemize.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a house with a small chart and a key. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Direct and indirect
segments.narration: Two kinds of costs go into the regular method. Direct expenses are only for the office, like painting it or fixing its window, and are deducted in full. Indirect expenses are for the whole home, like rent and utilities, and are deducted at your business-use percentage. Things that have nothing to do with the office, like landscaping or a renovation of the kitchen, don't count at all.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a paint roller in one room and a pie chart over a house. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The catch
segments.narration: The homeowner's catch is depreciation recapture. When you sell the home, the depreciation you were allowed on the office part is generally taxed, at up to twenty-five percent. And the office part may not qualify for the usual home-sale exclusion in some situations. Renters don't face this at all, and the simplified method avoids it for owners. If you plan to sell soon, it's worth a conversation with a preparer before choosing the regular method.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a for-sale sign next to a small coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Limit
segments.narration: One more rule for both methods: the deduction can't create or increase a business loss. With the regular method, any amount you can't use carries forward to next year. With the simplified method, it doesn't. So in a year with very low profit, the regular method can be better even if this year's deduction is capped. You can choose the method each year. For most freelancers with a steady profit this never bites, but in a first year with a small profit or a loss, it's worth knowing before you count on the deduction.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a ceiling line with an arrow to next year. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Audit myth
segments.narration: Is it a red flag? Plenty of legitimate businesses claim it every year. What causes trouble is claiming it without meeting the tests, or with an obviously inflated percentage. If your office really is used only for work, measured honestly, with records, you shouldn't fear it. Take a photo of the space, draw a simple floor plan with measurements, and keep twelve months of bills if you use the regular method.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a camera and a floor plan. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mileage bonus
segments.narration: There's a bonus most people miss. If your home office is your principal place of business, trips from home to clients, suppliers and the post office for work generally count as business miles, not commuting. So a qualifying home office can make your mileage deduction bigger too, at seventy-two and a half cents a mile for twenty twenty-six. That's next week's video.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a house with arrows to several places. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Moving
segments.narration: Two situations come up a lot. If you moved during the year, figure the deduction separately for each home, for the months you lived there, using that home's square footage and costs. And if you used the office for only part of the year, for example you started freelancing in April, the simplified method uses the average monthly square footage, and the regular method only counts the months the space qualified. Software walks you through both, but it helps to know why it's asking.
segments.on_screen_text: Moved or started mid-year? Split it
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two small houses with a calendar between them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: Here's the record kit that makes the deduction solid. A floor plan with the office and total home measurements. Two or three photos showing the space set up for work and nothing else. For the regular method, twelve months of rent or mortgage statements, utility bills and insurance. And a one-line note of what you do there and how often. Put it in this year's tax folder and you're done.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a folder with a floor plan and photos. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Choose
segments.narration: So how do you choose? Renters with a meaningful share of a high-rent home usually do better with the regular method. Small spaces, low costs, or owners who expect to sell soon often prefer the simplified method. Run both. It's a ten-minute calculation once you have your square footage and bills, and the difference can be several hundred dollars of tax a year.
segments.on_screen_text: Run both. Pick the better one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks being compared. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: This week
segments.narration: This week: measure your office and your home, take the photos, and work out both methods. It takes ten minutes, and you'll know exactly what your space is worth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tape measure and two small tags. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: you must be self-employed and use the space regularly and only for business, as your principal place of business. Simplified is five dollars a square foot up to fifteen hundred. Regular is your office share of real costs, plus depreciation for owners, who face recapture when they sell. It can't create a loss. And keep a photo, a floor plan and the bills. The Quarterly Tax Tracker in the description has the simplified home office built into its expense log. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: The mileage deduction: logs, rates, commuting rules and mistakes
script.hook: If you drive for your freelance work, your car might be one of your biggest deductions, and one of the easiest to lose. The rules aren't hard, but they're specific: which trips count, which method to use, and what the log needs to say. In this video we'll cover all of it with twenty twenty-six numbers, including the commuting rule that trips up most freelancers. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: If you drive for your freelance work, your car might be one of your biggest deductions, and one of the easiest to lose. The rules aren't hard, but they're specific: which trips count, which method to use, and what the log needs to say. In this video we'll cover all of it with twenty twenty-six numbers, including the commuting rule that trips up most freelancers. Education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes driving a small car along a curving road on a navy background. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Worth
segments.narration: First, why it matters. The standard mileage rate for twenty twenty-six is seventy-two and a half cents a mile. Three thousand business miles is a two thousand one hundred seventy-five dollar deduction. Eight thousand miles is fifty-eight hundred. At sixty thousand of profit, every thousand dollars of deductions saves about two hundred thirty dollars of federal tax, so eight thousand miles is worth over thirteen hundred dollars. That's real money for a notebook entry per trip. And unlike many deductions, it reduces both your self-employment tax and your income tax, because it lowers your business profit directly.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a road turning into a coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Which trips
segments.narration: Which trips count? Driving from one work location to another: from a client to a supplier, between two clients, to a business meeting, to the bank or post office for business, to a conference. Trips to pick up supplies. Trips to a temporary work site. What doesn't count: personal errands, and commuting. A useful test is to ask why you made the trip. If the answer is a client, a supplier, or a task for the business, it's probably a business trip. If the answer is anything else, it probably isn't.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map with several pins, some greyed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Commuting
segments.narration: Commuting is driving between your home and your regular place of work. It's personal, even if you take calls on the way. For an employee, that's the trip to the office. For a freelancer who rents a desk at a coworking space as their main workplace, the trip to that desk is usually commuting too. This is where many freelancers accidentally overclaim.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a car between a house and a building, greyed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Home office rule
segments.narration: But here's the rule that helps freelancers. If your home is your principal place of business, because you have a qualifying home office, then trips from home to clients and other business stops are generally business trips, starting from your front door. The home office is your base. That's one reason the home office tests from last week's video matter beyond the home office deduction itself.
segments.on_screen_text: Home office = trips from home count
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a house in the center with arrows to many places. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Standard rate
segments.narration: Now the two methods. The standard mileage rate is simple: business miles times seventy-two and a half cents. It's meant to cover gas, maintenance, insurance, registration and depreciation. On top of it you can still deduct business parking and tolls, and the business share of interest on a car loan. You can't also deduct gas or repairs; the rate already includes them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a road with mile markers and a parking sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Actual
segments.narration: The actual expense method adds up every real cost of the car for the year, gas, insurance, repairs, tires, registration, lease payments or depreciation, then multiplies by your business-use percentage. Business miles divided by total miles. Eight thousand of twenty thousand is forty percent. If total costs were eight thousand dollars, that's thirty-two hundred, much less than fifty-eight hundred with the standard rate.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a pie chart over a pile of car bills. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Choosing
segments.narration: So which is better? For an average car with average costs, the standard rate usually wins and is far less paperwork. Actual can win for an expensive vehicle with high costs and high business use. One important rule: for a car you own, if you want the option of the standard rate, use it in the first year the car is used for business. If you start with actual and depreciation, you generally can't switch to the standard rate later for that car.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a fork in the road with a star on one side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The log
segments.narration: Either way, you need a log. For each trip: the date, where you went, the business purpose, and the miles. Plus your odometer reading at the start and end of the year, and your total miles. It should be made at the time, or soon after. A spreadsheet tab, a notes app or a mileage app all work. The format doesn't matter. The details and the timing do. Many people find it easiest to log trips at the end of each day, or to use an app that records drives automatically and lets them classify each one later.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a notebook with four neat columns. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Example rows
segments.narration: Here's what good entries look like. March third, Riverside Cafe, kickoff meeting for a brand project, fourteen point two miles. March fifth, office supply store, printer ink and paper, six point eight miles. Short, specific, and written that day. Compare that with an entry like 'client stuff, March, two hundred miles'. One of these holds up if anyone asks; the other doesn't.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two notebook entries side by side, one crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rebuilding
segments.narration: If you didn't keep a log this year, you can reconstruct one, honestly, from your calendar, client emails, invoices and phone location history, with distances from a map app. Note that it was reconstructed and from what. Leave out trips you can't support. A smaller number you can back up beats a bigger number you can't. Then start a same-day log from today.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes piecing together map fragments. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: The mistakes we see most: claiming commuting miles. Claiming a round number with no log. Claiming a hundred percent business use of the only family car. Deducting gas on top of the standard rate. And forgetting parking and tolls, which are allowed on top. Avoid those and this deduction is both valuable and safe.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. five small crossed-out icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mixed trips
segments.narration: What about trips that mix business and personal? Say you drive to a client meeting, then go to the grocery store, then home. The business part is the trip to the client and the direct return, not the detour. A good habit is to log the business route only. And if a trip is mainly personal, like a vacation where you meet a client for coffee, it's generally not a business trip at all, though the specific business expenses during it may be.
segments.on_screen_text: Mixed trips: log the business route
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a route with one detour greyed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Two cars
segments.narration: If you have more than one car, keep a log per car, and use the method that fits each one. If you lease, the standard rate works too, but you must use it for the entire lease period once you choose it. If you sell or trade a car you depreciated under the actual method, that can create a gain or loss to report. These are the edge cases where a preparer earns their fee.
segments.on_screen_text: Two cars or a lease: special rules
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two small cars side by side with a key. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rideshare
segments.narration: A note for gig drivers and delivery workers: the same rules apply, but your business miles start when you're logged in and heading to a pickup, and the apps often give you an annual summary of on-trip miles that misses the miles driving to the first pickup or between orders. Your own log, or a mileage app running all shift, usually captures more of the miles you're entitled to deduct.
segments.on_screen_text: Gig drivers: log all shift miles
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a phone with a map and a small car. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where it goes
segments.narration: On your return, car expenses go on the car and truck line of Schedule C, and you answer a few questions about the vehicle: when you started using it for business, total miles, business miles, commuting miles, and whether you have written evidence. Those questions are a hint about what the IRS cares about. Make sure you can answer yes to the evidence question.
segments.on_screen_text: Schedule C car line + vehicle questions
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a small car icon. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Start today
segments.narration: If you take one thing from this video, start a same-day mileage log today, even a single note in your phone, and keep it for the whole year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes starting a fresh notebook. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: business trips count, commuting doesn't, and a qualifying home office makes trips from home count. The standard rate is seventy-two and a half cents a mile for twenty twenty-six, plus parking and tolls. Actual expenses times business use can win for expensive cars, but choose the standard rate in the car's first year if you want the option. And keep a same-day log. segments.heading: Example
segments.narration: Our freelancer is single, with sixty thousand dollars of Schedule C profit, no other income, and four estimated payments of sixteen hundred twenty-five during the year, sixty-five hundred in total. We'll start from that profit, because we covered how to get it, line by line, in our Schedule C video.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a profile card with four coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Schedule SE
segments.narration: Step one: Schedule SE. The profit times ninety-two point three five percent is fifty-five thousand four hundred ten. Twelve point four percent of that for Social Security is about six thousand eight hundred seventy. Two point nine percent for Medicare is about sixteen hundred seven. Total self-employment tax: about eight thousand four hundred seventy-eight. That number goes to Schedule two, and half of it, about four thousand two hundred thirty-nine, goes to Schedule one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with two arrows leaving it. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Schedule 1
segments.narration: Step two: Schedule one, additional income and adjustments. The business profit, sixty thousand, goes in the income part. The half of self-employment tax goes in the adjustments part, along with things like a SEP IRA contribution or self-employed health insurance if you have them. So our freelancer's adjusted gross income is sixty thousand minus four thousand two hundred thirty-nine: about fifty-five thousand seven hundred sixty-one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a plus and a minus. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deductions
segments.narration: Step three: from adjusted gross income, take the standard deduction, sixteen thousand one hundred for a single filer in twenty twenty-six, leaving about thirty-nine thousand six hundred sixty-one. Then Form eighty-nine ninety-five, the qualified business income deduction: twenty percent of the business income, capped at twenty percent of that thirty-nine thousand six hundred sixty-one, so about seven thousand nine hundred thirty-two. Taxable income: about thirty-one thousand seven hundred twenty-nine.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a stack with two slices removed. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Income tax
segments.narration: Step four: income tax on thirty-one thousand seven hundred twenty-nine, using the twenty twenty-six brackets. Ten percent on the first twelve thousand four hundred, twelve percent on the rest: about three thousand five hundred fifty-nine. That's the line most people think of as their tax. For a freelancer, it's the smaller part.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small staircase of two steps. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Schedule 2
segments.narration: Step five: Schedule two adds other taxes, and self-employment tax is the big one: eight thousand four hundred seventy-eight. Added to income tax, the total tax is about twelve thousand thirty-seven. That total tax line is important for another reason: it's next year's safe harbor number for estimated payments.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two stacks being combined. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Payments
segments.narration: Step six: payments. The four estimated payments, sixty-five hundred, go on the ten forty as payments already made, the same way an employee's withholding does. Any overpayment applied from last year counts too. Total tax of twelve thousand thirty-seven minus sixty-five hundred paid leaves about five thousand five hundred thirty-seven to pay by April fifteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a balance scale with coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Penalty
segments.narration: Step seven: was there an underpayment penalty? Our freelancer paid the safe harbor, a quarter of last year's sixty-five hundred, on time each quarter, so generally no. If payments were late or short, Form twenty-two ten works out the penalty; software usually does it for you, and the annualized method on that form can reduce it if your income came in late in the year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small meter at zero. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: W-2 too
segments.narration: What changes if you also have a W-2 job? Your wages go on the ten forty's first line, and your employer's withholding goes in the payments section next to your estimated payments. On Schedule SE, your wages count toward the Social Security wage base first, which only matters at high incomes. And because your business profit sits on top of your salary, it's taxed at your higher bracket. Software handles all of it, but this is why side income often needs a higher set-aside than you expect.
segments.on_screen_text: W-2 too: wages + withholding join in
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a briefcase joining the stack of forms. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Married
segments.narration: If you're married filing jointly, the standard deduction doubles to thirty-two thousand two hundred and the brackets are wider, so income tax is usually lower. But self-employment tax doesn't change: it's per person. If both spouses freelance, each has their own Schedule C and Schedule SE. And the QBI deduction is figured on the combined return. Check the joint numbers in software before deciding anything else.
segments.on_screen_text: Married: wider brackets, same SE tax
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two figures holding one form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health and retirement
segments.narration: Two adjustments are worth adding to the example. If our freelancer had paid five thousand dollars of health insurance premiums on their own plan, the self-employed health insurance deduction would reduce adjusted gross income on Schedule one, saving roughly four hundred eighty dollars. And a SEP IRA contribution of about eleven thousand one hundred fifty would save around a thousand seventy. Neither reduces self-employment tax, but both lower the income tax line we calculated.
segments.on_screen_text: SE health + SEP: lower income tax
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a medical shield and a plant pot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Refund or owe
segments.narration: What if the return shows a refund? That means your payments were more than your total tax. You can take the refund, or apply some or all of it to next year's first estimated payment. If you owe, you can pay through Direct Pay or your online account, and you can file early and schedule the payment for April fifteenth. Either way, look at the result against what you set aside, and adjust your percentage for the new year.
segments.on_screen_text: Refund: take it or apply it forward
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin boomeranging back. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Other forms
segments.narration: Other forms you might see: Form eighty-eight twenty-nine for the regular home office method, Form forty-five sixty-two for depreciation, Form seventy-two oh six for self-employed health insurance, and Form eighty-nine sixty for the additional Medicare tax at high incomes. And your state return, which usually starts from your federal adjusted gross income.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a few small forms in a fan. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Then there's your state return. Most states start from your federal adjusted gross income, the fifty-five thousand seven hundred sixty-one in our example, and then apply their own adjustments, deductions and rates. A few have no income tax at all. Some cities add their own tax. If you made state estimated payments, they go on the state return, not the federal one. Software usually carries the federal numbers over, but read the state summary as carefully as the federal one, because state notices are just as common.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline next to a second form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Effective rate
segments.narration: One more useful number to pull out of the return: your effective rate. Total federal tax, twelve thousand thirty-seven, divided by profit, sixty thousand, is about twenty percent. That's the number to plan your set-aside around, not your bracket. Add your state's effective rate, and you know exactly what percentage of each client payment belongs in the tax account this year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a dial pointing near 20. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Checks
segments.narration: Before you file, check four numbers against your own records. Schedule C gross receipts against your income log and your ten ninety-nines. Net profit against what you expected. Estimated payments against your IRS online account. And total tax against your estimate from the year. If any of them surprise you, find out why before you submit. Most errors are a typo or a missing payment.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a checklist with four lines. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Next year
segments.narration: And one number to carry forward: total tax, twelve thousand thirty-seven. Divided by four, that's about three thousand nine each quarter for twenty twenty-seven under the safe harbor, starting April fifteenth, the same day as this year's balance. For a first-year freelancer, that's the double payment we've talked about, so plan the cash for both.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a new calendar with four coins. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: Schedule C gives profit. Schedule SE turns it into self-employment tax. Schedule one adds the profit and subtracts half of that tax. The standard deduction and the QBI deduction give taxable income. The brackets give income tax. Schedule two adds self-employment tax. Your estimated payments come off, and the rest is due in April. Our free calculator in the description runs this whole chain for your numbers. Next time your software shows you a summary, you'll know exactly where every number came from, and which ones to double-check. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

script.title: 12 freelance tax mistakes that lead to IRS letters
script.hook: Most IRS letters to freelancers aren't audits. They're automated: a computer noticed something didn't match, or something was missing. The good news is that the same dozen mistakes cause most of them, and every one is avoidable. In this video we'll go through twelve, grouped into income, expenses, payments and paperwork, and how to fix each one before you file. Twenty twenty-six returns. Education, not tax advice.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Most IRS letters to freelancers aren't audits. They're automated: a computer noticed something didn't match, or something was missing. The good news is that the same dozen mistakes cause most of them, and every one is avoidable. In this video we'll go through twelve, grouped into income, expenses, payments and paperwork, and how to fix each one before you file. Twenty twenty-six returns. Education, not tax advice.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding an envelope with a small exclamation mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 1 Missing income
segments.narration: Mistake one: leaving out income that was reported on a ten ninety-nine. The IRS gets a copy of every NEC and K, and its matching program compares them with your return. If a client reported paying you five thousand and your return doesn't seem to include it, you'll get a notice proposing more tax. Fix: build your income from a log of every payment, then check that every ten ninety-nine is covered. This is by far the most common notice freelancers receive, and the easiest to prevent.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form and a ledger with a gap between them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 2 Net vs gross
segments.narration: Mistake two: reporting net instead of gross. A ten ninety-nine K shows the gross amount before platform fees. If you report only what landed in your bank, your income looks smaller than the form. Fix: report gross receipts and list the fees as an expense. Same tax, no mismatch.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin with a slice cut out next to a full coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 3 No form income
segments.narration: Mistake three: thinking income without a form isn't taxable. Clients who paid you under two thousand dollars, or paid by card, may send nothing. It's still income. The mismatch program won't catch it, but an audit would, and the penalties then are much bigger than the tax. Fix: same income log.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an empty mailbox next to a full ledger. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 4 Personal expenses
segments.narration: Mistake four: personal costs in business categories. Groceries as supplies, the family vacation as travel, your entire phone bill. These don't trigger automated letters, but they're the first thing an examiner looks at. Fix: only ordinary and necessary business costs, the business share of mixed costs, with a note for anything that isn't obvious.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shopping cart and a suitcase greyed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 5 Round numbers
segments.narration: Mistake five: round, unsupported numbers. Car expenses of exactly five thousand, meals of exactly two thousand. Real records rarely produce round numbers. Fix: total your actual records, even if the result is a less satisfying number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a perfectly round coin with a question mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 6 Home office
segments.narration: Mistake six: a home office that doesn't qualify. The space must be used regularly and only for business, as your principal place of business. Fix: if it doesn't meet the tests, don't claim it. If it does, keep a photo, measurements and, for the regular method, a year of bills.
segments.on_screen_text: 6. A home office that doesn't qualify
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a desk next to a bed, crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 7 Mileage
segments.narration: Mistake seven: mileage without a log, or with commuting miles mixed in. Fix: a log with date, destination, purpose and miles, written at the time; no trips between home and a regular workplace unless your home is your principal place of business.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an empty notebook next to a car. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 8 Payments
segments.narration: Mistake eight: missing or misdated estimated payments. You claim four payments but the IRS only has three, or one was applied to the wrong tax year. The result is a notice saying you owe more, plus a penalty. Fix: before filing, check your IRS online account for every payment and its tax year, and enter exactly what's there. Keep every confirmation number in one place during the year, so this check takes two minutes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four coins with one in the wrong box. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 9 Wrong year
segments.narration: Mistake nine, closely related: paying the January estimate under the new tax year. The January fifteenth payment is for the previous year. If it lands in the wrong year, one year looks underpaid and the other overpaid. Fix: if it happened, contact the IRS to move the payment before you file.
segments.on_screen_text: 9. January paid to the wrong year
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a dropdown with the wrong year highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 10 Contractors
segments.narration: Mistake ten: not sending ten ninety-nines you owed. If you paid a contractor two thousand dollars or more directly for services in twenty twenty-six, you were supposed to send a ten ninety-nine NEC by February first. Schedule C asks about it. Fix: file it now through the IRS's IRIS system; penalties are smaller the sooner you do.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form not yet in an envelope. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 11 Typos
segments.narration: Mistake eleven: simple typos. A wrong Social Security number for a dependent, a transposed digit in your bank account for the refund, the wrong filing status. Fix: read the summary page slowly before you submit. Software checks math, not whether the number you typed is right. Also double-check your name and taxpayer number match exactly what the Social Security Administration has on file, especially after a name change.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a magnifying glass over a single digit. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: 12 Ignoring letters
segments.narration: Mistake twelve: ignoring a letter when one arrives. Notices have response deadlines, and if you miss them, the proposed change becomes final. Most are easy to resolve with records. Fix: find the notice number, look it up on irs.gov, and respond by the deadline, agreeing or sending your evidence. And remember: the IRS starts with mail, never with texts, social media or gift card demands.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an unopened envelope with a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: CP2000
segments.narration: Since so many of these lead to the same letter, let's look at it. The most common notice for freelancers is a CP two thousand. It says the income on information returns doesn't match your return, and proposes a change: more income, more tax, maybe a penalty and interest. It is not a bill, and it is not an audit. You can agree, partly agree, or disagree, and you respond by the date on the letter, with copies of your records. Often the explanation is simple, like a ten ninety-nine K that included personal transfers, and the IRS accepts it.
segments.on_screen_text: CP2000: a proposal, not a bill
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a letter with a small balance scale. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Amend
segments.narration: What if you spot a mistake after you've filed, before the IRS does? You can fix it with an amended return, Form ten forty X. If you left out income, amending and paying quickly limits interest and penalties. If you missed deductions, amending can get you a refund, generally within three years of filing. Wait until your original return has been processed first, and don't amend for simple math errors the IRS will correct itself.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a small pencil correction. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Audit
segments.narration: And what about an actual audit? They're relatively rare, and most are by mail, asking for documents to support a few specific items, like car expenses or a home office. The same records answer them. If you ever get one and feel out of your depth, an enrolled agent or CPA can represent you, and the cost is a deductible business expense for the business part.
segments.on_screen_text: Audits: mostly by mail, records answer them
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a letter with a small folder attached. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Scams
segments.narration: One last warning, because tax season is scam season. The IRS doesn't text you, message you on social media, threaten arrest on the phone, or ask for payment by gift card, crypto or wire. If something claims to be the IRS and wants money now, stop, and check your account directly at irs.gov. Fake tax-help sites and fake refund emails are common too. When in doubt, type irs.gov yourself instead of clicking.
segments.on_screen_text: The IRS never texts or wants gift cards
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a phone with a crossed-out gift card. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Prevention
segments.narration: Notice that almost every fix is the same three habits: an income log, an expense log with notes, and a quick check of your IRS account before filing. With those, most letters never happen, and the ones that do take ten minutes to answer. That's the whole point of a simple system.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small notebooks in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Before you file
segments.narration: Here's a two-minute pre-filing routine that catches most of these. Line up every ten ninety-nine against your income log. Look at each expense category for anything personal or round. Confirm your home office and mileage meet the rules. Check your four estimated payments in your IRS account. Read the summary page for typos. Then file.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a short checklist with five ticks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: report all income at gross, matched to every ten ninety-nine. Only real business expenses, with records and no round guesses. A home office and mileage that meet the rules. Estimated payments that match the IRS's records and the right year. Ten ninety-nines you owed, sent. No typos. And never ignore a letter. The Quarterly Tax Tracker in the description keeps the logs that prevent most of these. Do the two-minute routine before you press submit, and most of these letters will simply never be written.
